nameStory: The 'rusty-rock' name perfectly captures this lichen's appearance - it looks like iron rust has stained the rock surface where it grows. The scientific name 'atrata' means 'clothed in black,' referring to the dark fruiting bodies that dot its rusty surface like tiny black buttons.
description: Rusty-rock lichen is a crusty, flat lichen that forms thin patches directly on rock surfaces, looking almost like the rock itself has been painted with rust-colored stains. It grows as a crustose lichen, meaning it's tightly bonded to its rocky home and can't be peeled off without damaging it. Individual patches typically spread 1-3 inches across, though several patches may merge to cover larger areas.

idTips.label: Rusty orange color
idTips.description: The thallus (lichen body) displays a distinctive rusty orange to reddish-brown color that looks exactly like iron oxide staining on rock

idTips.label: Crusty texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and gritty like sandpaper when you run your finger across it, completely fused to the rock surface

idTips.label: Black fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Small, round, jet-black dots (apothecia) scattered across the orange surface like tiny coal specks

idTips.label: Rock-hugging growth
idTips.description: Forms thin, flat patches that follow every contour and crack of the rock surface beneath

idTips.label: Smooth margins
idTips.description: Edges of the lichen patches blend smoothly into the rock without raised borders or obvious boundaries

habitat: Look for rusty-rock lichen on exposed granite, quartzite, and other hard acidic rock surfaces in New England's mountains and rocky outcrops. It thrives in areas with clean air and plenty of sunlight, often found on cliff faces, large boulders, and rocky summits above treeline. You're most likely to spot it in places like New Hampshire's White Mountains or Vermont's Green Mountains where hard bedrock is exposed.

seasonality.spring: Most visible after snow melt when rocks are clean and wet, making the rusty color particularly vibrant against dark, moisture-darkened stone.
seasonality.summer: Colors may appear slightly faded in intense sunlight, but black fruiting bodies are most prominent during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Often at its most colorful as cooler, moister conditions bring out the rich orange-rust tones in the thallus.
seasonality.winter: Still visible under snow, though colors appear muted; look for it on south-facing rock surfaces that get winter sun exposure.

funFact: This lichen is so perfectly adapted to harsh mountain conditions that it can literally freeze solid in winter and continue growing normally when it thaws - scientists have found it actively photosynthesizing at temperatures just above freezing when most other organisms have shut down completely.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with actual rust stains on metal or iron-rich rock surfaces. The key difference: real rust wipes off or flakes away when scraped, while rusty-rock lichen is firmly attached and often has those telltale black fruiting dots that metal rust never has.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertain claim flagged**: This is a very rare lichen in New England with only 2 recorded observations, so field identification should be verified by experts. Many crusty orange lichens exist, and proper identification often requires chemical testing or microscopic examination that's beyond typical field identification.
compareHints: **Uncertain claim flagged**: Since there are no other Tremolecia species recorded in New England, compare it with other orange crusty lichens in the region. Unlike the more common Caloplaca species which tend to be brighter yellow-orange, rusty-rock lichen has a deeper, more rust-like coloration and typically grows in harsher, more exposed mountain environments.
